title: Building a Bilingual Mathematical Brain
author: Fantastic Maths
summary: This article frames mathematical symbol fluency as a bilingualism problem: students must learn to read, write, and think in a second language — the language of mathematical notation — and the teaching methods that work for language acquisition also work for symbol fluency. The author argues for see-and-say choral response as the equivalent of phonics for mathematical symbols: a direct, high-repetition, low-inference method for building automatic recognition. Mnemonic shortcuts like the 'crocodile eats the bigger number' approach to inequality symbols are critiqued as creating cognitive traffic jams — students must decode the mnemonic before they can access the mathematical concept. A 'bimodal bilingualism' model is proposed, in which students develop fluency in both verbal and symbolic registers simultaneously. The article concludes that symbol fluency is an equity issue: students who lack automatic recognition of basic notation spend cognitive load on decoding that should be available for reasoning.
points: Mathematical symbol fluency is a language acquisition problem, not a conceptual one — students need the same high-repetition, direct-instruction methods that work for reading to develop automatic symbol recognition.

The 'crocodile eats the bigger number' mnemonic creates a cognitive traffic jam: students must first decode the mnemonic, then translate it to the symbol, before they can engage with the mathematics — adding processing steps that fluency should eliminate.
See-and-say choral response — the mathematical equivalent of phonics — builds the automatic recognition that lets students focus cognitive resources on reasoning rather than symbol decoding.

A bimodal bilingualism model holds that students should develop fluency in verbal and symbolic registers simultaneously, not sequentially, so they can move fluidly between informal and formal mathematical language.

Symbol fluency is an equity issue: students who lack it must spend working memory on decoding that their more fluent peers can direct toward problem-solving, compounding disadvantage at every level of the curriculum.
quotes: We teach children to read by giving them lots of practice reading. We do not teach them to read by giving them a story about why letters look the way they do. Mathematical symbols need the same treatment.
The crocodile is not helping. Every time a student invokes it, they are adding two cognitive steps between the symbol and its meaning. That is not a scaffold. That is a detour.
Mathematical notation is a second language. Like all second languages, it requires immersion, repetition, and production — not explanation.
Students who cannot automatically recognise basic mathematical notation are carrying a cognitive load that their peers are not. That is a disadvantage that compounds at every stage.
